title: How do you handle schema evolution in a data pipeline (Avro/Parquet schemas, a Schema Registry, backward/forward compatibility rules), and why do columnar formats like Parquet matter for analytics (column pruning, predicate pushdown, compression)?
shortTitle: Schema evolution in a data pipeline and why columnar formats matter
keyPoints: Schema evolution manages changes to data structure over time without breaking producers or consumers.
Avro embeds the writer's schema in the file header; Parquet embeds its schema in the file footer.
A Schema Registry stores versioned schemas and enforces backward, forward, or full compatibility rules.
Safe changes: add fields with defaults, deprecate old fields. Unsafe: rename in place, change types.
Column pruning lets Parquet read only the columns a query needs, cutting I/O by orders of magnitude.
Predicate pushdown uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip irrelevant data without decompression.
Same-type column values compress far better than mixed-type rows, reducing both storage cost and scan time.

s1_definition.oneliner: Evolve schemas safely with versioned formats, a registry, and compatibility rules; use columnar Parquet so analytics prunes columns, pushes down filters, and compresses hard.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Schema evolution** – managing changes to data structure over time (adding, removing, or changing fields) without breaking existing producers or consumers.
- **Schema Registry** – a central service that stores every version of each schema and enforces compatibility rules at registration time.
- **Backward compatibility** – a new schema can read data written with the old schema (new consumer, old data).
- **Forward compatibility** – an old schema can read data written with the new schema (old consumer, new data).
- **Column pruning** – reading only the columns a query needs from a columnar file, skipping the rest entirely.
- **Predicate pushdown** – using per-block min/max statistics to skip blocks that cannot match a filter.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps changing its transaction slip over the years: one year they add a "channel" field for mobile versus branch, another year they drop an unused box. Schema evolution is making sure an old reader can still process a new slip and a new reader can still process an old slip, so nothing breaks when the form changes. The Schema Registry is the central rule book holding every version of the slip and refusing a change that would break existing staff. And storing slips column by column, like Parquet, is like filing all the amounts in one slim folder, so totalling amounts means grabbing one folder instead of flipping through every full slip.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Schema Evolution in a Kafka Pipeline
  ────────────────────────────────────
  Producer                 Registry               Consumer
  ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────┐
  │ Serialize│────────▶│ Store schema │◀───────│Deserialize│
  │ with     │  register│ Version 1   │  fetch  │ with     │
  │ schema v2│         │ Version 2   │         │ schema v2│
  └──────────┘         │ (compat     │         └──────────┘
       │               │  rules)     │              │
       ▼               └──────────────┘              ▼
  [schema_id + payload]                    [payload -> record]
```

```text
  Columnar Format Benefits (Parquet)
  ──────────────────────────────────
  Row-Store (CSV/OLTP)           Column-Store (Parquet)
  ┌───────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ id|amt|dt|branch  │          │ id:  1, 2, 3, ...    │
  │ id|amt|dt|branch  │          │ amt: 100, 200, ...   │
  │ id|amt|dt|branch  │          │ dt:  Oct, Oct, ...   │
  │ (read ALL columns │          │ branch: Mum, Del,... │
  │  for any query)   │          │                      │
  └───────────────────┘          │ SELECT SUM(amt) reads│
                                 │ ONLY the amt column  │
                                 └──────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Schema evolution is managing changes to data structure over time without breaking existing producers or consumers. Handle it with self-describing formats like Avro for streaming and Parquet for storage, a Schema Registry that stores versioned schemas, and compatibility rules enforced at registration. The core rules are backward compatibility where a new schema can read old data, forward compatibility where an old schema can read new data, and full compatibility which is both. The practical discipline is to add fields only with defaults, never rename in place but instead add and deprecate, and never change a field's type incompatibly.

Columnar formats like Parquet matter for a related but separate reason: analytical performance and cost. Because Parquet stores data by column, a query reads only the columns it needs (column pruning), uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip blocks that cannot match a filter (predicate pushdown), and compresses same-type values dramatically better than mixed-type rows. Sort order makes min/max statistics effective by producing tight, non-overlapping ranges per block.

In a banking context at the National Bank of India, when the team added a channel field to transaction events to distinguish mobile from branch, they added it with a default so old consumers kept working and new consumers read it, and the Schema Registry rejected a careless change that would have added a mandatory field with no default. On the storage side, transaction history lived in sorted Parquet, so analysts totalling amounts read only the amount column and skipped irrelevant date partitions.

Parquet's embedded, evolvable schema let the table gain the new column without rewriting history, which is exactly the combination a growing bank system needs.

Remember one sentence: evolve schemas safely with a registry and compatibility rules, and use columnar Parquet so analytics reads only the columns it needs and skips irrelevant blocks.
